content.text: The International Space Station orbits Earth at an altitude of approximately $330\,\mathrm{km}$. Another satellite, Meteosat, is in geostationary orbit at an altitude of $36\,000\,\mathrm{km}$.
Which of the following correctly compares the orbital velocity and orbital period of these satellites?
Satellite 1: International Space Station; Satellite 2: Meteosat. The ISS has the greater orbital velocity and Meteosat the shorter orbital period.
Satellite 1: International Space Station; Satellite 2: Meteosat. The ISS has the lesser orbital velocity and Meteosat the shorter orbital period.
Satellite 1: International Space Station; Satellite 2: Meteosat. The ISS has the greater orbital velocity and Meteosat the longer orbital period.
Satellite 1: International Space Station; Satellite 2: Meteosat. The ISS has the lesser orbital velocity and Meteosat the longer orbital period.
Both satellites orbit the same central mass, so apply Kepler's law of periods, $\frac{r^3}{T^2} = \text{constant}$.

For a circular orbit $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$. Note which of the two satellites has the smaller orbital radius, remembering that the ISS's $330\,\mathrm{km}$ and Meteosat's $36\,000\,\mathrm{km}$ are altitudes, not radii.
C

Both satellites orbit the same central mass, so Kepler's law of periods $\frac{r^{3}}{T^{2}} = \text{constant}$ applies. The orbital radii are not the altitudes given: $r_{\mathrm{ISS}} = 6.37\times10^{6} + 0.33\times10^{6} \approx 6.70\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$ and $r_{\mathrm{Meteosat}} = 6.37\times10^{6} + 36\times10^{6} \approx 4.24\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m}$.

Orbital period: $T^{2} \propto r^{3}$, so the far larger radius of Meteosat gives it the much longer period, about $24\,\mathrm{h}$ compared with about $90\,\mathrm{min}$ for the ISS. Meteosat has the longer period.

Orbital velocity: for a circular orbit $v_{\mathrm{orb}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$, so the smaller radius of the ISS gives it the greater orbital velocity, about $7.7\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ compared with $3.1\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ for Meteosat.
The ISS has the greater orbital velocity and Meteosat the longer orbital period, which is option C.

items: 1 mark: selects option C

content.text: Which of the following best describes Galileo's analysis of projectile motion?
A projectile launched with a great enough velocity would escape Earth's gravity.
A projectile would travel in a straight line until it ran out of momentum, then it would fall.
A projectile launched from the equator towards the east with a great enough velocity would orbit Earth.
A projectile would travel in a parabolic path because it has constant horizontal velocity and constant vertical acceleration.
Galileo's key insight was that the horizontal and vertical parts of a projectile's motion could be treated separately and independently.
Ask what stays constant in the horizontal direction and what the acceleration is in the vertical direction, then combine the two to describe the shape of the resulting path.
D

Galileo showed that the horizontal component of the velocity of a projectile remains constant while the vertical component changes uniformly under gravity, so the path is a parabola. This rules out A, B and C.

content.text: A scientist at a particle accelerator laboratory observes the lifetime of a particular subatomic particle to be $1.0 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s}$ when it is travelling at $0.9999\,c$.

$1.4 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{s}$
$4.5 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{s}$
$1.0 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s}$
$7.1 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{s}$
Time dilation is $t = t_0\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}$, which gives the dilated interval measured by an observer who sees the clock moving.

The laboratory observer sees the particle moving, so the lifetime quoted in the question is the dilated one. The rest-frame lifetime is a factor of $\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}$ smaller than that, and you can check the size of that factor before substituting.

Time dilation means the laboratory observer sees a dilated lifetime, so the rest-frame lifetime is shorter than the observed value. This is option A.

content.text: A ball was thrown upward at an angle of $45^{\circ}$. It landed at the same height as thrown.
Which graph best represents the kinetic energy of the ball during its time of flight?

content.alt_text: Graph of kinetic energy $E_k$ against time $t$. The curve rises smoothly from a positive value to a rounded peak near the middle of the flight then falls smoothly back to a positive value.
Graph of kinetic energy $E_k$ against time $t$. The curve starts high, falls smoothly to a minimum at about the middle of the flight then rises smoothly back to a high value at the end.
Graph of kinetic energy $E_k$ against time $t$. The curve falls in straight lines to zero at about the middle of the flight then rises in straight lines back up.

Graph of kinetic energy $E_k$ against time $t$. A single straight line falls from a high value at the start of the flight, crosses the time axis near the middle and continues to a low value at the end.

content.text: Kinetic energy is $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, so track the total speed of the ball, not just its vertical component.
The ball leaves and lands at the same height, so compare the speeds at the two ends of the flight, and remember that the horizontal component of the velocity never changes.

The ball leaves and lands at the same height, so it has the same speed and hence the same kinetic energy at both ends of the flight, making the graph symmetric.

At the top of the trajectory the vertical velocity component is zero, so the kinetic energy is at a minimum, not zero, because the horizontal component is unchanged. A smooth curve that starts high, dips to a minimum midway and rises again is graph B.

content.text: Which statement about the Michelson-Morley experiment is correct?
It was a valid experiment because it tested the principle of relativity.
It was a valid experiment because it took into account the known properties of light.
It was an invalid experiment because it did not take into account the particle nature of light.
It was an invalid experiment because the speed of Earth through the aether was not taken into account.
The null result was not evidence that the experiment was badly designed, so ask which of the offered reasons makes the experiment a valid test rather than an invalid one.

Sort the options by what they refer to: the sensitivity of the instrument, the theory of light being tested, the nature of light itself, or the frame of reference. Only one of these explains why the result was trustworthy.
B
Michelson and Morley were testing for the 'aether wind'. Maxwell's theory of electromagnetism, based on the known properties of light, predicted that such a wind should be detectable.
Their interferometer was sensitive enough to detect it, but no fringe shift was observed, so the experiment was valid and produced a null result. Option B is the correct statement.

content.text: While drilling into a tough material, the DC motor in an electric drill is slowed significantly. This causes its coils to overheat.
Why do the coils overheat?
The resistance of the coils increases significantly.
The increased friction on the drill is converted to heat.
The back emf decreases and so the current in the coils increases.
The induced eddy currents increase and so more heat is produced.
A motor whose coil is turning in a magnetic field generates a back emf that opposes the supply, so for the motor alone $V = IR + \varepsilon_{\text{back}}$.

Decide what happens to the back emf when the rotor slows, and then use $I = \frac{V - \varepsilon_{\text{back}}}{R}$ to see how the current in the coils responds, remembering that the heating goes as $I^2R$.
C
A rotating motor generates a back emf that opposes the supply voltage. The back emf is proportional to the speed of the rotor, so when the drill is slowed the back emf falls.
With the supply voltage unchanged, a smaller back emf leaves a larger net voltage across the coil resistance, so a larger current flows and $I^2R$ heating increases. This is option C.

content.text: Why is high voltage used to transmit electrical energy from power stations to users?
It helps to protect the system from lightning strikes.
It allows the supporting structures to have smaller insulators.
It minimises the effects of the electrical resistance of the wires.
It ensures that, even with voltage losses, 240 V will still reach the user.
For a fixed power to be delivered, $P = VI$ ties the transmission current directly to the transmission voltage.
The energy lost in the transmission lines is $E_{\text{loss}} = I^2Rt$. Look carefully at how that expression depends on the current before choosing an option.
C
For a fixed transmitted power, $P = VI$, so raising the voltage lowers the current that must be carried in the transmission lines.

The energy lost in the lines is $E_{\mathrm{loss}} = I^2Rt$, which depends on the square of the current. Reducing the current therefore greatly reduces resistive heating in the wires, so C is correct.

content.text: The terminal velocity ($v_t$) of a spherical object in Earth's atmosphere is proportional to the square root of its radius ($r$).
Which graph correctly shows this relationship?

content.alt_text: Graph of terminal velocity $v_t$ against radius $r$. A single straight line rises from the origin with a shallow gradient.

content.text: A power relationship only looks like a straight line through the origin if a transformed quantity is plotted. Rewrite $v_t \propto r^{1/2}$ in the form $y \propto x$ and decide what has to be squared.
Squaring a power of $\tfrac{1}{2}$ cancels it, so squaring the quantity on the vertical axis turns this square-root relationship into a linear one.

B
$v_t \propto \sqrt{r}$ so $v_t^{2} \propto r$. Squaring both axes gives a straight line through the origin.

Only option B plots $v_t^{2}$ on the vertical axis against $r$ on the horizontal axis with a straight line, so B is correct. A and C plot $v_t$ itself, and D plots $\sqrt{v_t}$ against $r$, none of which is linear.

content.text: What was Max Planck's contribution to the development of quantum physics?
He combined the quantised wave and particle models of light.
He analysed the photoelectric effect and described light as quantised energy packets.
He explained black body radiation and the photoelectric effect using quantised energy.
He hypothesised that the radiation emitted and absorbed by the walls of a black body cavity is quantised.
Planck was trying to explain the spectrum of the radiation emitted by a hot cavity, not the photoelectric effect.
His assumption was that the oscillators in the wall of the cavity could exchange energy only in discrete amounts, $E = hf$, rather than continuously.
D
Planck explained black body radiation by assuming that the oscillators in the cavity wall could only exchange energy in discrete packets, quanta, of size $E = hf$.
He did not analyse the photoelectric effect (Einstein) and he did not combine the wave and particle models (that came later with Einstein and Bohr), so D is correct.

content.text: Heinrich Hertz devised and performed an experiment to investigate electromagnetic waves. In this experiment he was able to determine the speed of the waves.
Which method was used to determine the speed?
Timing how long it took the wave to travel a known distance.
Producing a wave of known wavelength and using reflection to determine the frequency.
Producing a wave of known frequency and using interference to determine the wavelength.
Using an interference pattern to determine the distance travelled and time taken.
A speed needs two quantities: $v = f\lambda$. Decide which of the two Hertz could set independently.
His spark-gap transmitter was an oscillator, so its frequency was fixed by the oscillator and effectively known; the reflector set up a standing wave whose nodes gave the wavelength.
C
Hertz used a spark-gap oscillator driven by an induction coil, so the frequency of the transmitter was set by the oscillator's natural frequency and was known.

He measured the wavelength of the standing wave formed between the transmitter and a reflecting loop antenna using an interferometer, then combined the known frequency with $v = f\lambda$ to get the speed, which matched the predicted value. This is option C.

content.text: If the magnitude of the magnetic field were doubled and the other variables were kept constant, what would the new radius be?
Equate the magnetic force to the centripetal force: $qvB = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$.
Rearrange to $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$ and ask what happens to $r$ when only $B$ is changed while $m$, $v$ and $q$ stay the same.
Sanity check the direction of the dependence: a stronger field bends the path more sharply, so the radius must get smaller rather than larger.

Equating the magnetic force to the centripetal force gives $qvB = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$, so $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.
With $m$, $v$ and $q$ unchanged, $r \propto 1/B$, so doubling $B$ halves the radius. The new radius is $r/2$, which is option B.

content.text: Towards which point does the bright spot move?
The spot moves in the direction of the force on the electrons, and that force follows $F = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ with a negative $q$.
Magnetic field lines leave a north pole, so draw the field at the screen pointing away from the approaching magnet, and take the direction of the electron velocity from the axis of the tube.

content.text: What did William and Lawrence Bragg use X-rays to investigate?
The speed of light.
The emission of photoelectrons.
The crystal structure of materials.

The Braggs used the angles at which the diffracted X-rays appeared to work out the spacing of those layers — think about what that reveals about a solid.

The Braggs used the fact that X-rays are diffracted by the regularly spaced layers of atoms in a crystal. Measuring the angles of diffraction at different orders gave the spacing of the atomic planes, so they determined the crystal structure of materials, which is option C.

content.text: Why is pure copper a better electrical conductor than pure silicon?
Electrons move through copper in pairs.
Silicon contains fewer free electrons than copper.
Copper has a conduction band and silicon does not.
Copper atoms contain more electrons than silicon atoms.
Conductivity depends on how many charge carriers are free to move through the material, not on the total number of electrons in its atoms.
In a metal the outer electrons are delocalised over the whole lattice; in a semiconductor they are bound into covalent bonds unless promoted into the conduction band.
B

In a metal such as copper a large number of valence electrons are delocalised, so the material has many free charge carriers. In silicon, a semiconductor, the valence electrons are bound into covalent bonds and only a small number are promoted to the conduction band at room temperature.
Because silicon therefore has fewer free electrons than copper, its resistance is higher and it is a poorer conductor. This is option B.

content.text: Outline consequences of the space vehicle entering the atmosphere at angle A AND angle C.
The key quantity is how much of the atmosphere the vehicle passes through before its kinetic energy has been converted to heat, and that is set by the entry angle measured against the surface.

Work out the shallow-angle case first: what happens to a vehicle that meets only the very thin upper layers and so loses very little speed? Then do the opposite case, in which the vehicle plunges deep into dense air and sheds its energy in a very short time.

The vehicle's speed is essentially unchanged by gravity while it is high above the atmosphere, so what matters is the depth of atmosphere it can pass through before its speed is reduced enough. A shallow entry angle A means the vehicle only skims the upper, very thin layers, is deflected back out into space and does not land. A steep entry angle C means the vehicle plunges deep into the dense atmosphere and converts its kinetic energy into internal energy of the gas and of the vehicle in a very short time, so the vehicle burns up. Both consequences are the opposite of the controlled, gradual heating produced at the optimum angle B.

content.text: Why does the mass hang with the string at an angle to the vertical?
In the frame of the train the mass is stationary, so the tension must be opposed by the other forces; that is only possible if the tension has a horizontal component.

The mass hangs to one side of its suspension point. The horizontal component of the tension points back towards the suspension point, and that is the direction of the train's acceleration — the string leans towards the acceleration, not away from it.

The train must be accelerating towards the left, because the mass hangs to the right of its point of suspension and the horizontal component of the string tension - the only horizontal force on the mass - points back towards the suspension point. The train may therefore be moving to the right and slowing down, or moving to the left and speeding up. Only the tension has a horizontal component, so the resultant of the tension and the weight is not vertical, which is why the string hangs at an angle with the mass displaced opposite to the acceleration.
Work in the frame of the train. The mass is stationary there, so before the string breaks the resultant force on it is zero, and in the ground frame it has the same acceleration as the train.

Only two real forces act on the mass: its weight, vertically downwards, and the tension, along the string. The weight has no horizontal component, so the horizontal component of the tension is the net horizontal force and it must point in the direction of the train's acceleration. For the resultant to vanish in the train's frame the tension must be tilted away from the vertical, so the string hangs at an angle and the mass is displaced to the side opposite the acceleration.

Read the direction off the figure rather than off the stem: the mass hangs to the right of its point of suspension, so the horizontal component of the tension points to the left, and the train is accelerating to the left. The diagram carries no marker for the direction of travel, so no more specific statement is possible. This is the official answer: 'The train must be accelerating toward the left. content.text: The string then breaks and the mass falls.
Indicate the path of the mass on the diagram above. Explain why the mass has taken this path.
Sketch the path in the frame of the train, where the mass is at rest at the instant the string breaks.
Once the tension is gone the mass accelerates in the direction of the force that was previously balancing the tension — work out how that direction sits relative to the string.

A path leaving the mass along the line of the string, downwards and to the right, curving so that it becomes progressively steeper until the mass is falling vertically. The path does not rise, and no landing point can be given because the diagram does not mark the direction in which the train is travelling.

In the frame of the train the mass is stationary before the string breaks, so the net force on it is zero. Two things are therefore in balance: the tension, which acts along the string towards the ceiling, and the combined effect of the weight and the train's acceleration, which acts along the line of the string in the opposite direction.

The moment the string breaks the tension is removed and nothing else about the situation changes, so the mass must now accelerate along the line of the string, in the direction of the forces that were opposing the tension. On this figure that is downwards and away from the point of suspension, that is downwards and to the right. This is the official reasoning: 'In the frame of the train the acceleration of the mass is zero, hence there is zero net force. Therefore, apart from the force applied by the string there must be opposing forces. When the string breaks the force exerted by the string is removed and the mass must accelerate in the direction of those opposing forces, which must be along the line of the string' (2010 HSC Physics Sample Answers, p.3).

In components, the vertical component of that acceleration is $g$ downwards, supplied by the weight, and the horizontal component is the apparent force produced by the train accelerating to the left, which acts to the right in the frame of the train. The same motion described in the ground frame is: once the string has broken no horizontal force acts on the mass, so it keeps the horizontal velocity of the train, and it thereafter accelerates vertically downwards at $g$.

The sketch on the diagram therefore starts at the mass, heading along the line of the string downwards and to the right, and becomes progressively steeper as the downwards velocity builds, so that the mass ends up falling vertically. It does not rise, and the direction of travel is not marked, so no landing point can be specified. This matches the sample-answer figure, which draws the path leaving the mass along the string and curving down towards the vertical.

content.text: In 2014 the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) will be placed in orbit around the Sun. Earth and the JWST will follow the orbits shown, with identical orbital periods.

content.alt_text: Concentric circular orbits around a shaded circle labelled Sun. A large filled dot labelled Earth sits on the inner orbit and a small dot labelled JWST sits on the outer orbit on the same side of the Sun. The words NOT TO SCALE appear at the right.

content.text: This appears to contradict Kepler's law of periods.
Why is it possible for the JWST to orbit the Sun with the same orbital period as Earth? In your answer, refer to Kepler's law of periods.
Write Kepler's law of periods as it is normally quoted, and identify the assumption hidden behind it: that the orbiting body feels a gravitational force from a single central mass.

Ask whether that assumption holds for the JWST. The diagram places the JWST just beyond the Earth and on the same side of the Sun, so list every massive body that is exerting a gravitational force on it.
Then apply the law using the total central mass rather than the Sun's mass alone, and check whether a larger central mass allows the same orbital period at a larger radius.

Both the Sun and the Earth exert a gravitational force on the JWST, so the mass acting at the centre of the JWST's orbit is greater than the Sun's mass alone. Kepler's law of periods $r^{2}/T^{2} = GM/4\pi^{2}$ therefore allows a larger orbital radius for the same period.

Kepler's law of periods, $r^{2}/T^{2} = \text{constant}$, is derived on the assumption that the orbiting body experiences a gravitational force from a single central mass. That assumption is valid for the Earth, whose orbit is dominated by the Sun, but it is not valid for the JWST, whose orbit lies just beyond the Earth and which is strongly attracted to the Earth as well as to the Sun.

The gravitational forces of the Sun and the Earth both act on the JWST, so the mass at the centre of the orbit is effectively $M_{\mathrm{Sun}} + M_{\mathrm{Earth}}$, which is greater than $M_{\mathrm{Sun}}$. From $T^{2} = \dfrac{4\pi^{2} r^{3}}{G(M_{\mathrm{Sun}} + M_{\mathrm{Earth}})}$ a larger total central mass allows a larger orbital radius for the same period, which is exactly the relationship shown. The larger radius of the JWST is therefore balanced by the extra central mass, so there is no contradiction with Kepler's law.

content.text: How does the law of conservation of momentum apply to the motion of the rocket?
Choose the system first: the rocket together with the exhaust gases, with no significant external force acting on it.
Apply Newton's third law at the nozzle and let conservation of momentum follow from it.

The momentum of the burnt fuel and the momentum of the rocket are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, produced by an equal and opposite pair of forces between the rocket and its exhaust, so the total momentum of the rocket plus fuel is conserved.

In the frame of the rocket the only significant interaction producing thrust is between the rocket and the exhaust gases leaving the nozzle. The rocket pushes the gases backwards out of the nozzle, so by Newton's third law the gases push the rocket forwards with an equal and opposite force. The change in momentum of the gas is therefore equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the change in momentum of the rocket, so the total momentum of the system is conserved. The rocket gains forward momentum as the exhaust gains backward momentum, which is why the rocket continues to accelerate upwards after the fuel has left the nozzle.

content.text: Why do the g-forces on an astronaut in the rocket differ at times $t_1$ and $t_2$?
Separate what stays constant (the engine thrust) from what changes (the mass, which the graph shows falling).
The g-force on the astronaut is set by the support force from the floor, and that depends on the rocket's acceleration: $a = F_{\text{net}}/m$.
The g-force is larger at $t_2$ than at $t_1$, because the engine thrust is constant but the mass of the rocket is smaller, so $a = F/m$ and the apparent g-force $1 + a/g$ are both larger at $t_2$.

The astronaut feels the normal force exerted by the seat or the floor of the rocket. The engine thrust is constant throughout the burn, so the net force on the rocket, $F_{\mathrm{thrust}} - mg$, increases as the mass $m$ decreases, and by $F_{\mathrm{net}} = ma$ the acceleration of the rocket therefore increases as the fuel is burnt. The apparent g-force experienced by the astronaut is $1 + a/g$, so it is greater at $t_2$ than at $t_1$, when the rocket is still heavier. The increasing acceleration is what the falling mass-time graph in the question is intended to highlight.

content.text: Magnetic resonance imaging is a current technology that uses superconductors.
Identify two OTHER technologies that use superconductors. Evaluate the impact of these technologies on society and the environment.

MRI is excluded, so choose two technologies from different fields if you can — for example a large research facility such as a particle accelerator, transport such as a maglev train, or an instrument such as a SQUID magnetometer.

For each technology you need one specific point about its impact on society or the environment, not a general statement: name the capability that superconductors provide, and then the benefit or the cost that follows from that capability.

The marking scheme requires a point for each of the two applications plus a clear judgement on at least one of them, so make the judgement explicitly and support it with the impacts already described, including any cost such as the refrigeration energy or the mining of the superconducting materials.

Any two of: particle accelerators such as the Large Hadron Collider, maglev trains, SQUID magnetometers, and the magnets of experimental nuclear fusion reactors. Impact: these technologies have enabled major advances in medicine, physics and transport, but they require large quantities of energy to cool to very low temperatures, consume scarce materials such as niobium, and add to greenhouse gas emissions and mining impacts.

Superconductors have no electrical resistance, so very large currents can be carried without generating heat, which allows extremely strong magnetic fields to be produced in relatively small and light devices. A superconductor must be cooled below its critical temperature, so the technologies that exploit them in practice are those where a very strong field justifies the cost of refrigeration.

The Large Hadron Collider uses niobium-titanium superconducting magnets cooled in liquid helium to produce fields of several tesla, which allows protons to be accelerated to energies of teraelectronvolts. This has allowed physicists to probe the structure of matter at scales of $10^{-19}\,\mathrm{m}$ and has produced medical benefits such as the development of hadron cancer therapy, but the ring consumes a great deal of electricity to keep the magnets cold, and the mining and manufacture of niobium and titanium has its own environmental impacts. Maglev trains use superconducting magnets to levitate and drive the train, giving fast intercity travel with no wheel-on-rail contact, which reduces local noise and air pollution compared with conventional trains, but they require a large capital cost, continuous cryogenic cooling and a dedicated guideway, so whether the environmental benefit outweighs that cost is still debated. SQUID magnetometers, used in medical magnetocardiography and in non-destructive testing, and the magnets proposed for controlled nuclear fusion reactors, involve the same trade-off between capability and the environmental cost of refrigeration.

Overall the impact on society is strongly positive, because the field strengths achievable only with superconductors make technologies possible that cannot be built in any other way and they have delivered real medical, scientific and transport benefits. The environmental cost of cryogenic refrigeration, of the energy consumed and of the extraction of superconducting materials must nevertheless be weighed against those benefits, and it can be reduced by improving the efficiency of the refrigeration and by recycling the rare materials used.

content.text: Explain how the deflection plates produce this pattern.
A potential difference across a pair of parallel plates creates an electric field $E = V/d$, and the electron beam experiences the electric force $F = qE$.

There are two pairs of plates. Before explaining the shape of the trace, state what each pair does to the spot: one pair must account for the spot moving from side to side across the screen, the other for the spot moving up and down.

The repeated, evenly spaced shape of the trace comes from the voltage on the sweeping pair. Ask whether that voltage changes smoothly and continuously or in a series of jumps, and how the spot behaves during the jumps.

One pair of vertical plates, connected to a periodically varying ramp-like voltage, sweeps the beam horizontally so the spot moves across the screen at a constant rate. A second pair of horizontal plates, connected to the signal being studied, deflects the beam vertically by an amount proportional to that signal. The combination traces the signal waveform on the screen.

There are two pairs of parallel plates, one pair vertical and one pair horizontal, oriented so that each produces an electric field across the path of the electron beam. A potential difference across a pair of plates produces an electric field $E = V/d$, and this field exerts a force $F = qE$ on the electrons in the beam, deflecting them; the vertical plates deflect the beam horizontally and the horizontal plates deflect the beam vertically.

The pair of vertical plates is connected to a periodically varying, ramp-like voltage from the time base, so the horizontal deflection sweeps the spot steadily from left to right at a constant rate and then snaps back, which is why the trace is repeated regularly along the screen. The pair of horizontal plates is connected to the input signal, so the vertical deflection of the spot at any instant is proportional to the instantaneous value of that signal. As the beam sweeps across the screen, the vertical deflection follows the input, and for a sinusoidal input this draws the repeated sinusoidal trace shown on the screen.

content.text: Is the doped germanium an n-type or a p-type semiconductor? Justify your answer.
The type of a semiconductor is set by whether the dopant has more or fewer valence electrons than the host atom whose place it takes, so compare the two atoms directly.
An atom with one fewer outer electron than its neighbours cannot make all of its covalent bonds. The unfilled bond is a hole, and holes behave as positive charge carriers.
p-type, because boron has three valence electrons while germanium has four.

Germanium is a Group 14 element with four valence electrons, so in pure crystalline germanium each atom forms four covalent bonds with its neighbours and there are essentially no free charge carriers. Boron is a Group 13 element with only three valence electrons. When a boron atom is substituted into the lattice it forms only three covalent bonds, leaving one incomplete bond, or hole. Because the dominant charge carriers are these holes, which behave as positive charges moving through the crystal, the doped semiconductor is p-type.

content.text: Explain how the addition of boron alters the electrical conductivity of germanium.
Conductivity in a semiconductor is set by the number of mobile charge carriers, so compare how carriers are produced in the pure crystal with how they are produced once boron is present.
Ask in each case whether energy has to be supplied to free a charge carrier, and recall what happens to the resistivity when the carrier density rises.

The conductivity increases, because each boron atom creates a hole without the need for any energy input, giving a much greater number of mobile charge carriers than the very small number of electron-hole pairs present in pure germanium at room temperature.

In pure germanium, charge carriers are generated only when a valence electron gains enough energy from collisions or heat to break free of its covalent bond, leaving a hole behind. Because the band gap of germanium is relatively large, very few electron-hole pairs exist at room temperature, so the material conducts poorly. Each boron atom substituted into the lattice, however, creates a hole directly, without any energy input, and a valence electron from a neighbouring bond can drop into that hole, freeing itself and leaving a new hole behind, so the holes effectively move through the crystal and act as charge carriers. The greatly increased number of mobile charge carriers means a much greater current flows for the same electric field, so the conductivity increases and the resistivity of the doped germanium is much lower than that of pure germanium.

content.text: Explain why light having a wavelength longer than a certain value does not produce an electric current in a photocell.
Write the energy of a single photon as a function of its wavelength, $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, and note what happens to that energy as the wavelength increases.
Now consider what a single electron must gain in order to leave the metal surface, and how that requirement sets a longest wavelength at which emission just stops.

There is a threshold wavelength for the metal. Longer wavelengths give lower energy photons ($E = hf = hc/\lambda$), and when the photon energy is less than the work function of the metal no electrons are emitted from the surface, so no photoelectrons are produced and hence no photocurrent flows.

The energy of a photon is $E = hf = hc/\lambda$, so as the wavelength increases the energy of each individual photon decreases. In the photoelectric effect an electron is only emitted from the metal surface if it can absorb enough energy from a single photon to overcome the work function $\phi$ of the metal, the energy needed to escape from the surface. For photons with energy less than $\phi$ no electrons are emitted at all, however intense the light. Since $hc/\lambda \leq \phi$ defines a longest wavelength, the threshold or cut-off wavelength, any light with a wavelength greater than this threshold wavelength cannot liberate electrons from the photocell electrode, so no electrons are available to be collected by the anode and no electric current flows in the circuit. Increasing the intensity of such light only increases the number of low energy photons, which still cannot eject electrons, so the current remains zero.

content.text: Two significant problems that will affect a manned spaceflight to Mars are:

items: 1. the changes in gravitational energy
2. protecting the space vehicle from high-speed electrically charged particles from the Sun.

content.text: Use your understanding of physics to analyse each of these problems.

Handle the two problems separately, and for each one identify the conservation law or field relationship that is actually doing the work: the vehicle must climb out of the Sun's gravitational potential well, and it will be struck by fast charged particles.

Push each problem through to its consequences. For the energy problem, ask how much energy must be supplied and what that does to the mass that has to be launched; for the radiation problem, ask how much shielding is needed and what that does to the same launch mass.

A deep answer links the problems together rather than treating them as unrelated. Remember too that a spacecraft moving through a magnetic field can have large potential differences induced across it, by the law of electromagnetic induction.

Changes in gravitational energy: the Sun's gravitational field and the gravitational potential energy of the vehicle both fall steeply with distance, so the vehicle must climb out of a deep potential well; a vehicle starting at rest relative to the Sun needs at least the escape velocity of the solar system, which requires a large fuel mass. Charged particles: high-speed charged particles from the Sun and the interplanetary magnetic field produce ionising radiation, material damage and induced emfs; the vehicle needs substantial shielding, which adds directly to the launch mass problem, or active shielding with superconductor magnets, which is heavy and consumes power.

Changes in gravitational energy. The gravitational field strength due to the Sun is $g = GM_{\odot}/r^{2}$ and the gravitational potential energy of a mass $m$ is $U = -GM_{\odot}m/r$, so both fall steeply as the vehicle moves away from the Sun. The energy change needed to climb from low Earth orbit to the orbit of Mars is of the order of the gravitational potential energy of the vehicle at Earth, so a large amount of energy must be supplied. From the law of conservation of energy, a vehicle that starts at rest relative to the Sun can only leave the solar system if its total mechanical energy is positive, which requires a speed of at least the escape velocity $v = \sqrt{2GM_{\odot}/r}$ of about $42\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ at Earth's orbit. Because that energy must be carried as the kinetic energy of the vehicle itself, a very large fuel mass must be launched, and much of that fuel is used simply to reach orbit, so the launch mass and cost escalate. Radiation and micrometeorite damage during the long cruise compound these problems.

High-speed electrically charged particles from the Sun. The Sun emits a stream of charged particles, the solar wind, and its magnetic field accelerates charged particles to very high energies. These particles carry large kinetic energies and charge, so when they strike the hull of the vehicle they ionise and damage surface material, degrade electronics and are a serious hazard to the crew, whose cells they can also damage. A spacecraft moving through the interplanetary magnetic field is also subject to the induced emf described by Faraday's law, so a moving conductor can have large potential differences induced across it, which can cause electrical arcing and damage. The only protection is shielding. Passive shielding requires a very large mass of dense material, which adds directly to the launch mass problem described above, creating a vicious circle. Active shielding, using very strong magnetic fields produced by superconducting magnets to deflect the charged particles, avoids the mass but consumes large amounts of power to keep the magnets cold, and introduces its own engineering and reliability risks. Either way, the vehicle mass, energy requirement and cost rise, and the risk to human life is unacceptable if the shielding is inadequate.

(ii) Observations of the period of a pendulum on a ship show variations with location. Explain how these observations could be used to deduce information about the shape of Earth. Your answer must include a description of the shape of Earth.

(iii) The period of a pendulum is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$. The period of a particular pendulum is measured at one location as 2.00 seconds. When measured at a second location the period is 2.05 seconds.
(iii) Determine the ratio of the strength of the gravitational field at the first location to that at the second location.

For the first sub-part this is a list question: name the measurable properties of earth materials that geophysicists actually use, and do not include things such as chemical composition that cannot be measured directly on a rock sample in the field.

For the second, write the pendulum period formula and the field formula, eliminate the length of the pendulum, and remember the answer must include a description of the shape of Earth as well as the reasoning that leads to it.
For the ratio, notice that it is the same pendulum at both locations, so the length cancels and you can go straight from the two periods to the ratio of the two field strengths.

items: (a)(i) Any three of: density, elasticity (or rigidity), seismic wave velocity, electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, magnetic susceptibility, radioactivity, viscosity, fluidity, compressibility, porosity.

(a)(ii) Earth is an oblate spheroid, flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator. Since $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$ for a fixed pendulum, the period is longer where $g$ is smaller. The measured period is smallest at the poles and greatest at the equator, and because $g = GM/r^2$ this shows the radius of Earth is smallest at the poles and largest at the equator.

content.text: Part (a)(i) is a recall question about the properties geophysicists measure, and any three correct ones earn the mark. The list is deliberately about measurable responses rather than about chemistry.

Part (a)(ii) requires two equations. For a pendulum of fixed length $l$ in a uniform field, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$, so the period of one unchanged pendulum is controlled only by the local $g$. Since $g = GM/r^2$ for a spherically symmetric Earth, the period is a direct measure of the distance of the surface from Earth's centre, that is of the local radius. Surveying $T$ at known latitudes around the world therefore maps the local radius. The measured variation is that $T$ increases from the poles towards the equator, so $g$ decreases and the radius increases in that direction. That rules out a sphere and identifies the shape as an oblate spheroid, flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator, which is the shape expected for a rotating body.

Part (a)(iii) therefore has no unknown except the ratio itself: the length cancels because the pendulum was not changed, so the only thing that changed was the field, and the result is dimensionless. The field at the first location is about 5 per cent greater than at the second, as expected for two sea-level locations at different latitudes.

content.text: How are gravity measurements used to obtain information about the structure of Earth?

Set out the chain in order: how the local value of $g$ is measured, what has to be corrected for before the readings mean anything, what the corrected value is then compared against, and what a difference between the two reveals about the rock below.

Keep two ideas apart as you write: $g$ depends on mass and on distance, so denser rock and a smaller radius both raise it; and because the interpretation of any anomaly is not unique, gravity data always have to be combined with seismic and geological data.

Accurate gravimeters are used to survey the variation of $g$ over the Earth's surface by aircraft, ships and land surveys, and by satellite. The raw readings are reduced by correcting for latitude, altitude, topography, tidal effects and instrument calibration, after which maps of the gravity anomaly are produced. Comparing the measured $g$ with the value expected for a uniform sphere of the same mass and radius, using $g = GM/r^{2}$, reveals departures from that model. These anomalies are caused by lateral variations in the density of the rock beneath the surface, so the survey data are used to infer the boundaries and depths of layers of different density, such as sedimentary basins, the thickness of the continental crust, the Moho discontinuity, the core-mantle boundary and the shape of the core. Gravity data are also used to locate ore and hydrocarbon deposits and to monitor changes in ground water.

A gravimeter is a sensitive instrument that measures the local value of the gravitational field strength $g$. Modern instruments such as superconducting and absolute gravimeters use a suspended mass whose position changes slightly as $g$ changes, and can resolve very small variations. Because $g$ decreases with distance from the centre of Earth and is also affected by the mass of material beneath the instrument, a survey of $g$ over the Earth's surface, carried out on land, at sea and from aircraft, and now also from satellites using precision orbit determination, produces a detailed map of the variations in $g$.

The raw data must be reduced before they can be interpreted. Corrections must be applied for the effect of latitude and altitude, for the topographic elevation of the station, for tidal changes in $g$ due to the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun, for the free-air and Bouguer corrections which remove the effect of the surrounding terrain, and for the calibration of the instrument. The corrected values are then compared with the value of $g$ expected for a homogeneous sphere of the Earth's mass and radius using $g = GM/r^{2}$. The difference between the measured and the expected value at each location is the gravity anomaly, and a map of these anomalies is plotted.

A gravity anomaly arises wherever the density of the rock differs from the average density, because $g$ depends on both the mass and the distance. A body of denser material such as an ore body or a mafic intrusion produces a positive anomaly, while a body of less dense material such as a water-filled sedimentary basin produces a negative anomaly. The size and shape of the anomaly, combined with the survey geometry and with the way the anomaly changes with distance, allows the position, depth and shape of the density contrast to be calculated, usually with a computer model. Repeating this process over a whole continent has allowed the major density interfaces of the Earth to be mapped, including the sedimentary basins, the thickness of the continental crust, the Moho discontinuity between crust and mantle, the core-mantle boundary at about 2900 km and the inner core. Gravity data are also used in exploration to locate ore bodies and in hydrology to monitor changes in ground water. A significant limitation is that gravity is a very weak field, so the measurements are easily masked by surrounding effects, the interpretation of an anomaly is not unique, and gravity data must always be interpreted together with seismic, magnetic and geological data.

items: (c)(i) P waves are longitudinal compressional waves, are faster than S waves, can travel through both solids and liquids, and are refracted as they pass between layers of different density. S waves are transverse shear waves, are slower than P waves, and can travel through solids only, not through liquids.

(c)(ii) $v_S$ is zero in a liquid and increases with depth, increasing faster than it would if only $\rho$ changed; $v_P$ also increases with depth but more slowly than $v_S$; $v_P > v_S$ always; and $v_P$ is not zero in a liquid, so P waves travel through both solids and liquids.

(c)(iii) The S wave is drawn passing straight through the liquid outer core, which is impossible because $v_S = \sqrt{\mu/\rho}$ is zero in a liquid, so the S wave must be refracted or totally reflected at the core-mantle boundary. The P wave is drawn as a straight line, undeflected at the core-mantle boundary, which is also incorrect because P waves refract whenever they cross a boundary at which their speed changes, so its true path curves.

content.text: Part (c)(i): P waves are produced by compressions and rarefactions of the rock along the direction of travel, so they are longitudinal, and they are the faster of the two types, so they arrive first at a distant station. S waves are produced by the rock being displaced perpendicular to the direction of travel, so they are transverse, and because it is the rigidity of the material that resists transverse displacement they travel more slowly and cannot propagate through a liquid at all, since a liquid has no shear rigidity. P waves can travel through liquids, so they can pass through the outer core, whereas S waves cannot. Both are refracted at boundaries where their speed changes, and it is that refraction which makes the internal structure of the Earth deducible.

Part (c)(ii) has to be read out of the equations. From $v_S = \sqrt{\mu/\rho}$: $\mu$ is zero for a liquid, so $v_S = 0$ there and S waves cannot cross a liquid; both $\mu$ and $\rho$ increase with depth, so $v_S$ increases with depth; and because $\mu$ increases at a faster rate than $\rho$, the ratio $\mu/\rho$ increases, so $v_S$ increases faster than a change in density alone would give.

The same reasoning applied to $v_P$ gives three more conclusions. Because $K$ and $\mu$ both increase with depth, the numerator increases, so $v_P$ also increases with depth, but more slowly than $v_S$ because the density in the denominator does not fall. Since $K + \tfrac{4}{3}\mu > \mu$ for all positive values, $v_P > v_S$ everywhere both waves can exist, so P waves always arrive first. Finally $K$ is not zero in a liquid, so $v_P$ is not zero in a liquid and P waves travel through both solids and liquids. That last fact, combined with the absence of S waves at the antipode of an earthquake, is the evidence for a liquid outer core.

Part (c)(iii) tests the same two rules against the drawn paths. The drawn S wave runs in a straight line from $O$ through the centre of the Earth, crossing the core-mantle boundary and passing through the outer core. That is impossible because the outer core is a liquid and $v_S = 0$ in a liquid, so the S wave must be strongly refracted or totally reflected at the core-mantle boundary, leaving an S wave shadow zone on the opposite side of the Earth. The drawn P wave runs in a straight line from $O$ to the far side, undeflected at the core-mantle boundary, which is also wrong: both $K$ and $\mu$ change abruptly there so $v_P$ changes markedly, and the wave must change direction, curving towards the normal as it enters the faster core, with a P wave shadow zone at about $103^{\circ}$.

content.text: There is current acceptance of the idea that the continents have moved relative to each other.
Why was there initial reluctance to accept this idea, and what evidence led to its acceptance?

Separate the two demands of the question: the reasons for the initial reluctance, and the evidence that finally settled it. Do not mix them, and note that the marking guide requires you to link the evidence back to the specific objections it overcame.

The reluctance was methodological rather than observational, so look for the missing mechanism and the assumed age of the Earth. The decisive evidence came decades later, and the two key items are the symmetrical magnetic striping either side of the mid-ocean ridges and the measured youth of the ocean floor.

Reluctance: Wegener proposed continental drift but could give no convincing mechanism, and the age of the Earth was then thought to be only tens of thousands of years. Evidence: the fit of the continental shelves across the Atlantic, matching fossils and plant distributions, matching rock strata and mineral deposits, the discovery of sea-floor spreading and the young age of the ocean floor, measured movement of the sea floor, and the occurrence of earthquakes and volcanoes along plate boundaries rather than in the interiors of plates.

Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents had once been joined and had drifted apart. Despite the striking fit of the coastlines of South America and Africa, the matching of fossils such as Mesosaurus, the distribution of the plant Glossopteris and of coal measures, and the matching of rock strata and mineral deposits across the Atlantic, the idea met strong resistance. The main objections were that Wegener could not identify a physical mechanism capable of driving the slow horizontal movement of continents, and that the dominant view at the time was that the Earth was only about 6000 years old, which made the time available for such movement far too short. Continental drift was therefore regarded as speculation rather than evidence-based theory.

The breakthrough came in the 1960s with the invention of the magnetometer and of sonar for mapping the sea floor. Vine and Matthews showed that the ocean floor records a pattern of symmetrical magnetic stripes of alternating polarity on either side of the mid-ocean ridges, with the oldest rocks furthest from the ridge; this is exactly what is predicted if new sea floor is continuously created at the ridges and moves outwards. Sampling of the sea floor showed that it is very young, less than about 200 million years, compared with the billions of years of the continental rocks, which is impossible if the ocean basins were permanent. Seismic profiling revealed that the sea floor is created at mid-ocean ridges and consumed in deep ocean trenches at the edges of the oceans, providing precisely the mechanism that Wegener lacked. Modern satellite and laser measurements now show the continents moving at a few centimetres per year, comparable to the rate predicted from the sea floor spreading data, and earthquakes and volcanoes are found to be concentrated along the plate boundaries rather than in the interiors of the plates. Together these observations, combined with the earlier circumstantial evidence, led to the acceptance of the theory of plate tectonics and the abandonment of the idea of permanent continents.

content.text: Describe how an X-ray image of the bones in the hand is produced.
The image is a shadow image. Ask what reaches the detector where there is bone and what reaches it where there is only soft tissue.
Absorption depends on density and atomic number, so compare the calcium in bone with the water and soft tissue around it.

X-rays from a tube are directed at the hand. The dense calcium in the bone absorbs far more X-rays than the surrounding soft tissue, so fewer X-rays reach the photographic film or digital detector behind the hand where the bone is, and more reach it where there is only soft tissue. The film or detector records the varying intensity as differences in darkness, producing a shadow image of the bones.

X-rays are produced in an evacuated tube in which electrons are accelerated through a high potential difference and strike a tungsten target. The resulting X-rays are directed through the hand onto a photographic film, or onto a fluorescent screen that is then photographed, or onto a digital detector. X-rays are strongly absorbed by materials of high density and high atomic number, and the calcium in bone has a much higher density and atomic number than the water and soft tissue of the hand, so the bone absorbs a much greater fraction of the X-ray intensity than the soft tissue does.

Consequently the intensity of the X-ray beam reaching the film or detector is much lower where it has passed through bone than where it has passed only through soft tissue. The film is darkened according to the intensity of the radiation that reaches it, so the regions behind soft tissue become dark while the regions behind bone remain pale. The result is a shadow image, or radiograph, in which the shapes of the bones appear light against the darker surrounding tissue, and the degree of darkening indicates how absorbing the material is.

content.text: The half-life of Tc-99m is 6 hours.
A half-life is a trade-off: think about what is gained by the activity decaying quickly and what is lost because the isotope cannot be stored.
For the graph, remember that halving continues indefinitely - the mass approaches zero but never reaches it, so the curve is exponential and flattening, not a straight line down to the axis.

(i) Advantage: the patient is exposed to ionising radiation for a relatively short time, so the total dose is small and the isotope does not persist to irradiate the patient after the scan. Disadvantage: the isotope cannot be stockpiled; it must be manufactured close to the hospital and used almost immediately, which makes the supply chain difficult and the scan expensive. (ii) Plot $10\,\mathrm{g}$ at $0\,\mathrm{h}$, $5\,\mathrm{g}$ at $6\,\mathrm{h}$, $2.5\,\mathrm{g}$ at $12\,\mathrm{h}$ and $1.25\,\mathrm{g}$ at $18\,\mathrm{h}$, joined by a smooth exponential decay curve that halves every 6 hours and flattens towards, but never reaches, zero.

(i) A 6-hour half-life is long enough for a diagnostic scan to be completed, but short enough that the activity has decayed to negligible levels within a day or so, so the patient is not exposed to ionising radiation long after the scan. That is a clear advantage over longer-lived isotopes such as iodine-131, which continue to irradiate the body for weeks. The matching disadvantage is that the isotope cannot be stockpiled: the parent nuclide molybdenum-99 must be shipped to each hospital, the technetium-99m has a shelf life of only hours and must be supplied in kit form with sterile chemicals, and producing and delivering a short-lived isotope close to the point of use adds significantly to the cost and requires a very reliable supply chain.

content.text: Why is hydrogen the most commonly targeted element in the magnetic resonance imaging process?
Part (i) is about why one nucleus is chosen above all others for imaging - consider both how abundant it is in the body and what its nucleus is like.
Part (ii) asks what happens in three stages: what the static field does to the nuclei, what the radio frequency pulse does to them, and what they do when the oscillator is switched off.

Hydrogen is the most commonly targeted element because it is the most abundant element in the human body, mainly as water and fat, and because the hydrogen-1 nucleus is a single proton with a nuclear spin of $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and therefore a non-zero magnetic moment. The combination of very high abundance with a large magnetic moment gives by far the strongest signal and the best signal-to-noise ratio in a clinically acceptable scanning time.

Magnetic resonance imaging detects nuclei that have a net nuclear spin. The hydrogen-1 nucleus is a single proton, which has spin $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and therefore a magnetic moment, so it behaves as a tiny magnet and responds to the machine's static field. Two practical factors then make it the obvious choice: hydrogen is present in enormous quantities in the body, chiefly as water and as fat, so any small volume of tissue contains very many hydrogen nuclei; and among the abundant elements hydrogen-1 uniquely combines a spin of $\tfrac{1}{2}$, a large magnetic moment and high abundance. Other magnetic nuclei such as sodium-23, phosphorus-31 and carbon-13 are either less abundant, have a larger nucleus and hence a broader resonance line, or both. The image is therefore essentially a map of hydrogen density weighted by the relaxation properties that distinguish one tissue from another.

content.text: Describe how energy from the radio frequency oscillator of a magnetic resonance imaging machine interacts with hydrogen to obtain information about the inside of the body.

In the static magnetic field the hydrogen nuclei align with the field. The radio frequency oscillator then applies an RF field at the Lamor frequency, which the aligned nuclei absorb, tipping them out of alignment. When the oscillator is switched off the nuclei relax back towards their original alignment and re-emit the absorbed energy as radio waves at the same Lamor frequency; a receiving coil detects this signal, and its intensity and phase depend on the hydrogen density and on the relaxation times, which differ between tissue types, so the image shows the internal structure.

The patient lies in a strong static magnetic field. Within it the nuclear magnetic moments align with the field, splitting the hydrogen energy levels into a small number of separated states, and the nuclei precess about the field at the Lamor frequency $f = \gamma B/2\pi$. A radio frequency oscillator generates an alternating electric field at that resonant frequency, and a coil directs it into the body as a pulse. Nuclei whose moments are aligned with the static field absorb the RF energy, are excited to a higher level and are tipped out of alignment; the amount absorbed depends on the density of hydrogen nuclei, so tissues with different hydrogen content absorb different amounts of energy.

When the oscillator is switched off, the nuclei relax back towards their original alignment, losing the absorbed energy, and re-emit it as radio waves at the same Lamor frequency. The intensity and phase of this emitted signal depend on both the hydrogen density and on the relaxation times of the tissue, which differ from one tissue type to another. A receiving coil detects the signal, and the scanner measures its strength and phase at many positions and over many cycles, reconstructing an image in which each voxel shows the hydrogen density and relaxation properties of that region, so that the internal structure and any abnormality can be identified.

content.text: A cancer specialist has access to ultrasound, CAT and PET scanners.
Which of these technologies is the most appropriate to detect a 3 mm brain tumour? Justify your choice.

The three techniques do not measure the same thing: one shows anatomy, one shows function, and one depends on whether sound can reach the organ at all. Decide which of those properties the question actually needs before you compare resolutions.
Justifying a choice means naming it and then explicitly ruling the other two out with valid reasons.

CAT scanning. A tumour 3 mm across must be localised spatially, and CAT uses penetrating X-rays to produce cross-sectional images with a spatial resolution of about 1 mm. Ultrasound cannot be used because the skull blocks sound, and PET detects function but has a spatial resolution of only about 5 mm, so it cannot resolve a 3 mm tumour.

The three technologies differ fundamentally in what they measure and in their resolution. CT scanning sends penetrating X-rays through the head and measures how much is absorbed by the tissue along each line through the body, then reconstructs cross-sectional images from many such projections. It is therefore a structural, or anatomical, technique with a spatial resolution of about 1 mm, which is fine enough to show a 3 mm mass. In a scan with contrast medium the X-ray absorption of the tumour differs from that of the surrounding brain tissue, so the mass appears as a region of different density and can be located precisely in the images.

PET is of limited use here. PET works by detecting the gamma rays emitted by a positron-emitting radionuclide that has been taken up by the tissue, and relies on positron-electron annihilation photons rather than on any property of the tumour's size or density, so it is a functional technique. It is excellent for showing that a region has abnormal metabolism or that a known metastasis is present, but its intrinsic spatial resolution is only about 5 mm at best, and in practice a 3 mm lesion is at the limit of detection and cannot be reliably resolved or accurately localised, so PET would be used to characterise a lesion after CT has found it rather than to find a 3 mm tumour.

Conventional diagnostic ultrasound should be ruled out for this examination. Ultrasound is excellent for imaging soft tissue, but the adult skull is a thick, highly reflecting bone barrier and no ultrasound can be transmitted through it from outside, so no usable image of the adult brain can be obtained with a standard probe. Intra-cranial ultrasound is possible only through the fontanelle in an infant, or surgically through a trephine hole, which is not justified for a routine investigation. Ultrasound also has a limited resolution in brain tissue.

CAT is therefore the most appropriate choice, because it can penetrate the skull, provides the spatial resolution needed to detect and localise a 3 mm tumour, and is widely available and non-invasive.

content.text: The Japanese radio telescope HALCA was placed in an elliptical orbit which took it as far as $21\,000\,\mathrm{km}$ from Earth. It took measurements simultaneously with ground-based radio telescopes.
Explain the benefit that the HALCA telescope gives radio astronomers.

For the first sub-part the key word is that both instruments observed simultaneously. Ask what a pair of widely separated receivers observing the same source at the same instant amounts to, and how the angular resolution of that arrangement depends on their separation rather than on the size of either dish.

For the second sub-part there are two separate improvements available from flying at altitude, and the marking guide wants two: one concerns how much of the incoming signal reaches the detector at all, the other concerns how much irrelevant background reaches it along with the signal.

HALCA and the ground-based radio telescopes observing the same source at the same time act as a very long baseline interferometer. Their effective aperture is the enormous baseline between them, not the diameter of either telescope, so the angular resolution is far better than that of any single ground-based dish. This allows radio astronomers to resolve fine structure in radio galaxies, quasars and supernova remnants and to measure the positions of compact radio sources accurately enough to track their motion over decades. (a)
Part (a)

is about what an interferometer is. Two or more telescopes observing the same source at the same instant and combining their signals act as a single telescope whose effective diameter is the distance, the baseline, between them; the angular resolution then improves as the baseline increases, in contrast to an optical telescope whose resolution is limited by diffraction at the aperture of a single dish. Because radio wavelengths are long, a ground-based dish of any practical size has very poor angular resolution, so extending the baseline to a quarter of the Earth's diameter by putting one element in orbit gives a large improvement in resolving power, far beyond anything two ground stations can achieve coherently. The observational payoff is the ability to resolve jets and shock fronts in radio galaxies and quasars, to measure the angular sizes of compact sources such as pulsars, and to determine radio source positions accurately enough to follow their motion over decades.

content.text: SOFIA is an infrared telescope. It is operated from high-altitude aircraft.
Give TWO reasons for the greater validity of data from this telescope, compared with ground-based observations.

Infrared radiation is strongly absorbed by water vapour and carbon dioxide in the lower atmosphere, so operating above most of the water vapour means much more of the astronomical infrared signal reaches the detectors, giving a higher signal-to-noise ratio. Also, at altitude the telescope is above the strong thermal infrared emission from the ground and from the atmosphere, so the background against which the weak astronomical signal is measured is much lower, which improves the signal-to-noise ratio in a second, independent way.

has two distinct causes, and they should not be run together. The first is attenuation: water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb strongly in the infrared, so much of the astronomical signal is lost before it reaches a ground detector. Flying at about 13 km puts SOFIA above most of the water vapour, so a much greater fraction of the incoming infrared flux is collected, which raises the signal-to-noise ratio. The second is background: the Earth's surface at ordinary temperatures emits strongly in the thermal infrared and the atmosphere also emits, so a ground-based detector is swamped by this foreground. Flying above most of the emitting atmosphere and above much of the ground reduces the background, again raising the signal-to-noise ratio. Operating above the turbulent lower atmosphere also reduces the seeing that blurs images, but the two reasons required are the absorption and the background.

content.text: Properties of stars, including their surface temperature and chemical composition, can be measured by using their spectra.

For the first sub-part, list what a spectrum reveals besides composition and temperature: the line positions, widths, strengths and any overall shift each carry different information, and each points to a different stellar property.

For the second sub-part, separate the two jobs. Composition comes from the narrow dark lines, because each element absorbs at its own discrete set of frequencies. Temperature comes both from the continuous part of the spectrum and from how strongly and how deeply the lines are formed.

Trace the light outwards from the interior as you write: the continuous spectrum is generated deep inside the star, while the line spectrum is produced in the cooler, thinner outer layers. That split is what allows the composition question and the temperature question to be answered independently.

items: (b)(i) Any two of: the translational (radial) velocity of the star, from the Doppler shift of its spectral lines; the density of gas in the stellar atmosphere, from the strength and width of the absorption lines; the rotation of the star, from the broadening and distortion of the lines; the surface gravity, from the line widths; the magnetic field strength, from the splitting of the lines; and the age of the star.

(b)(ii) Composition: light generated deep in the stellar interior with a continuous, nearly black-body distribution of wavelengths passes outwards through layers of decreasing temperature and density. At the discrete frequencies at which an atom can absorb, photons are absorbed in the cool outer atmosphere, so those wavelengths are missing and appear as narrow dark absorption lines. Because atomic energy levels are quantised, each element has its own unique set of line frequencies, so the pattern identifies the elements present and the relative strengths of the lines give their relative abundances. Temperature: the continuous part of the spectrum follows the black-body curve for the photosphere, so the position of its peak gives the temperature by Wien's displacement law and its shape and width also depend on temperature; the lines give a second, independent measure, since a cool star shows many strong lines with the continuum peak in the red, a hotter star shows fewer and more strongly ionised lines with the peak moving towards shorter wavelengths, and in the hottest stars the continuum peak lies in the ultraviolet.

content.text: Part (b)(i): a stellar spectrum carries much more than temperature and composition. A star moves through space at tens of kilometres per second, so its light is Doppler shifted and the whole pattern of absorption lines is displaced towards the red or the blue; measuring that displacement gives the radial velocity, which is how the rotation of the Sun, the motion of stars about the centre of the Galaxy and the recession of distant galaxies were all measured. The widths and strengths of the lines are controlled by the state of the gas: high-pressure dense atmospheres give broad pressure-broadened lines and low-density atmospheres give sharp lines, so the density, the surface gravity and the rate of rotation of the star can be deduced, and a strong magnetic field splits and broadens the lines. Combined with the luminosity these also give an estimate of the radius and the age.

Part (b)(ii) begins with how the spectrum is made. Light is generated deep in the interior with a continuous, approximately black-body distribution of wavelengths and passes outwards through layers of decreasing temperature and density. The continuous curve therefore carries the information about the temperature of the layer from which the light last scattered, the photosphere, while the narrow features superimposed on it carry the composition.

Composition: at wavelengths where the gas is transparent the interior light passes straight through, but at the discrete frequencies at which an atom can absorb, photons are absorbed and scattered by the outer layers, so those wavelengths are missing from the spectrum and appear as dark lines. Because the energy levels of an atom are quantised, each element absorbs and emits only at its own particular set of frequencies, a unique fingerprint, so the observed pattern is compared with laboratory spectra and the elements present are identified. The relative strengths and widths of the lines depend on the number of atoms, the temperature and the pressure, so relative abundances can be calculated.

Temperature: the continuum is close to the black-body curve for the photosphere temperature, so Wien's displacement law applied to the peak gives the temperature, and the overall shape and width of the continuum also depend on it. The lines give an independent measure, because ionisation depends on temperature: a cool star is mostly neutral and its deep, cool atmosphere is opaque at many wavelengths, so the spectrum is crowded with strong lines and the continuum is visible only in small windows, with the peak in the red or infrared; as the temperature rises the atoms are progressively ionised, fewer strong lines are present, the remaining lines form higher in the atmosphere, and the continuum peak moves towards shorter wavelengths; in the hottest stars the hydrogen is ionised and only multiply charged species show lines, with the continuum peak in the ultraviolet. Comparing the appearance with known or model spectra therefore gives the surface temperature, which is what is plotted on the horizontal axis of an H-R diagram.

content.text: Read the two circled positions off the diagram before explaining anything. The vertical axis is luminosity and the horizontal axis is temperature (spectral type), so describe each region in those two terms first and name the class of star second.
For the energy question, ask in each case what is actually supplying the radiated power: a nuclear reaction, or the release of gravitational potential energy as the star contracts.

For the sketch, use the fact that all the stars in the cluster formed at the same time, so whatever is missing from the diagram must be the group that has already died. The survivors lie along the lower main sequence and in a branch bending away from it.

items: (c)(i) White dwarfs.

(c)(ii) As the mass of a main sequence star increases its luminosity increases, but its lifetime decreases. The most massive main sequence stars are therefore the most luminous and the shortest lived, while the least massive are the faintest and the longest lived.

(c)(iii) Stars in region W, the hot and very luminous stars on the main sequence at the top left, produce their energy by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores. Stars in region Z, the white dwarfs, do no appreciable fusion; they radiate the thermal energy stored in their interiors, which is supplied by slow gravitational contraction, and they are supported by electron degeneracy pressure rather than by gas pressure.

(c)(iv) A band of stars along the lower part of the main sequence, running from the bottom right up towards the left and ending at a clear turn-off point, with a branch running from the turn-off point away to the right and upwards; the top left of the diagram is completely empty.

content.text: Part (c)(i): region Z lies at the bottom left, where the luminosity is very low, about $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-4}$ of the Sun, while the spectral type is hot, B or A. The stars are therefore small and hot but faint, and only white dwarfs occupy this part of the diagram.

Part (c)(ii): along the main sequence the mass, luminosity, radius, temperature and lifetime all vary together. A main sequence star is in hydrostatic equilibrium, with the gravitational force on a shell of material balanced by the pressure produced by fusion in the core, so mass and luminosity are closely linked: a star several times more massive than the Sun has a much hotter core, fuses hydrogen far faster and radiates far more energy. But a greater fusion rate consumes the fuel faster, and the greater mass also loses more energy to neutrinos, so lifetime, roughly available fuel divided by consumption rate, falls steeply. The most massive main sequence stars are consequently the most luminous and the shortest lived.

Part (c)(iii): a main sequence star such as those in region W generates its energy by fusing hydrogen into helium in the core, with the pressure from that energy production balancing the inward gravitational force; because it is hot its surface temperature, colour and position on the spectral axis are high, towards the B or O end. A white dwarf has exhausted the nuclear fuel in its core, so it is not shining because of nuclear reactions; it radiates the thermal energy stored in its interior, supplied by slow gravitational contraction converting gravitational potential energy into internal energy. Being small it is faint, but because it is hot its colour is towards the blue end of the spectrum, which places it in the bottom left, region Z. With no fusion there is no outward pressure from energy production, so the star is supported entirely by electron degeneracy pressure.

Part (c)(iv): a globular cluster is an old, gravitationally bound collection of stars that formed at about the same time from the same material, so all its stars are essentially the same age and composition. Over billions of years the most massive and most luminous main sequence stars have already lived and died, so the cluster no longer contains the stars that lie at the top left of the diagram and that region is empty. The survivors lie in two groups: a band of stars along the lower main sequence running from the bottom right upwards to the left, and, above it, a red giant branch. Since the more massive stars leave the main sequence first, the highest-mass stars still on the main sequence form a distinct turn-off point, and the giant branch bends away to the right and upwards from that point.
