content.text: Identify THREE advances in measurement technologies, and describe how they have improved our understanding of celestial objects.

Choose three technologies that each improved a different thing: sensitivity, resolution, or the range of wavelengths available. For each one, state a specific thing astronomers can now do that they could not do before.

The marking guide awards its top band for identifying THREE advances and showing the relationship between each advance and the specific improvement in understanding, so avoid writing a bare list of names.

Any three of: photographic plates replaced by charge-coupled devices; adaptive optics; radio, infrared and optical interferometry including very long baseline interferometry; placing telescopes in space to avoid atmospheric absorption and distortion; larger and more accurate detectors; spectrographs and the extension of spectroscopy into the infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray and radio regions; and detectors for gravitational waves and neutrinos. Each has improved sensitivity, resolution, wavelength coverage or timing, and hence the accuracy of the measurements and the models built from them.

Measurement technology has repeatedly transformed astronomy, because every improvement in sensitivity, resolution or wavelength coverage changes the questions that can be answered. Three important advances illustrate this.

First, the replacement of photographic plates by charge-coupled devices greatly increased the sensitivity and linearity of detection. Photographic plates integrated light inefficiently and non-linearly and had to be replaced and measured by hand, whereas a CCD converts most of the arriving photons directly into electrons that can be counted and stored digitally. A faint star that would take an hour-long photographic exposure to detect is now recorded in seconds, so survey telescopes can record millions of stars over the whole sky. This has allowed the number counts of faint galaxies to be measured out to much greater distances and with much better statistical reliability, which is the direct observational evidence that the universe is expanding and that the number of galaxies was much smaller in the past.

Second, adaptive optics has largely removed the blurring caused by atmospheric turbulence for ground-based optical and infrared telescopes. A wavefront sensor measures the distortions of incoming starlight many times a second and a deformable mirror is continually adjusted to cancel them, so the images are limited by the diffraction of the telescope aperture rather than by the seeing. This makes it possible to image exoplanets directly, to resolve the details of galactic nuclei, to observe gravitational lensing and to follow stars as they orbit distant black holes, all of which are impossible with seeing-limited images.

Third, the extension of observation into wavelengths that the atmosphere blocks, together with the use of interferometry, has opened entirely new fields. Radio and millimetre observations reveal cold gas, dust and molecules that emit no visible light, including the cold molecular clouds in which stars form and the cosmic microwave background; infrared astronomy penetrates the dust that obscures the centres of galaxies; ultraviolet and X-ray astronomy shows the hot, high-energy gas in supernova remnants, accretion discs and hot galaxy clusters. Interferometry, in which telescopes separated by thousands of kilometres are combined, gives angular resolution far beyond that of any single dish, so the central compact object in a galaxy or the details of a distant quasar jet can be resolved, and the changing positions of masers and stars over decades can be measured to give direct evidence of black holes.

These advances have not simply produced more precise versions of the same pictures. Each has revealed populations of objects or regions that were previously invisible, and each has converted qualitative claims, such as the existence of exoplanets, dark matter, supermassive black holes and the cosmic microwave background, into quantitative measurements that can be tested against theory.

content.text: Outline the relationship between Bohr's atomic model and Planck's equation $E = hf$.
Start with what the model says: how many orbits are there, and what is special about the energy of the electron in each of them?
Now think about what has to happen if the electron moves from one orbit to another, and by what route that energy leaves or enters the atom.
Planck's equation relates the energy of a photon to its frequency, so the link between the two ideas is a statement about exactly when a photon is emitted or absorbed.

Bohr's model has electrons in a small number of stationary, non-radiating orbits, each with a definite quantised energy. An electron is only emitted or absorbed when it jumps between two such levels, and the energy of the photon involved equals the difference in energy between the two levels, $E = hf = E_2 - E_1$.

Bohr combined Planck's quantum hypothesis with Rutherford's nuclear model to produce a model of the hydrogen atom in which the electron moves in one of a small number of circular orbits at the centre of which sits the nucleus. The crucial feature is that only certain orbits are permitted; each allowed orbit has a definite, fixed total energy, so the electron does not radiate energy while it remains in any one of them and the atom is stable.

Transitions between the permitted orbits are also quantised. If an electron falls from a higher orbit to a lower one, the energy of the system decreases by a definite amount $\Delta E = E_2 - E_1$, and by the law of conservation of energy that energy must be carried away, in the form of a single photon whose quantised energy satisfies Planck's equation $E = hf = \Delta E$. Conversely, if the atom absorbs a photon whose energy is exactly equal to the difference between two permitted levels, the electron is promoted to the higher orbit. Since the energy levels are fixed and discrete, only particular discrete frequencies of light are absorbed or emitted by the atom, which is why hydrogen produces its characteristic line spectrum rather than a continuous one, and why Planck's equation and Bohr's model are inseparable parts of the same theory.

content.text: How did Louis de Broglie explain the stability of electron orbits in hydrogen atoms?
de Broglie's starting point was that matter, not only light, has a wave character. Write down the wavelength he gave for a particle of mass $m$ moving at speed $v$.

Apply that wavelength to an electron travelling round a nucleus and ask what must be true for the wave to be physically allowed - a travelling wave would interfere with itself unless the pattern closes.
Then make the final link: what is it about a standing wave that stops the electron radiating, and therefore stops the atom collapsing?

de Broglie proposed that the electron has a wave nature with wavelength $\lambda = h/mv$. An electron in a permitted orbit has a standing wave around the nucleus, so a whole number of wavelengths fits exactly into the circumference. Only such orbits are possible, so the electron does not radiate and the atom is stable.

de Broglie proposed in 1924 that the electron, like all matter, has a wave as well as a particle character, with a wavelength $\lambda = h/p$, where $p$ is the momentum. Applying this to the electron in the Bohr model, the electron wave travelling around the nucleus forms a standing wave: the circumference of each permitted orbit is occupied by a whole number of wavelengths, an integer standing wave, so the wave pattern closes on itself and forms a physically allowed stationary state.

Only orbits for which the circumference $2\pi r$ is a whole number of electron wavelengths, so that $2\pi r = n\lambda$, are permitted, and each of these has a definite energy. This is exactly equivalent to Bohr's condition that the angular momentum is quantised, and it explains his result rather than merely restating it. Since the electron occupies a stationary standing wave, it does not accelerate in the classical sense and therefore does not radiate energy, so the atom is stable and does not collapse. In the modern quantum mechanical picture the orbit is replaced by a standing wave in the three-dimensional electron probability cloud, and the allowed standing wave patterns are the electron's quantised energy levels.

content.text: How did Pauli account for the distribution of energies in the $\beta$-decay curve?

content.alt_text: Graph of the number of $\beta$-particles against the energy of $\beta$-particles. The curve rises steeply from the origin to a single rounded maximum and then falls smoothly away, approaching the horizontal axis at a marked value labelled Emax.

content.text: Read the shape of the curve first. It is continuous, running from nearly zero energy up to a marked maximum $E_{max}$, rather than being a set of separate lines.
Then ask what conservation of energy alone predicts for a decay that emits only one particle. If only the electron were emitted, what would its energy have to be, and why?
The resolution is a third product that carries away an unknown share of the released energy and momentum, and that is invisible both to the apparatus and, for a very long time, to experiment.

Pauli proposed that a third particle, the neutrino, is emitted in every $\beta$-decay and carries away part of the released energy and momentum. Because the neutrino is electrically neutral and interacts only very weakly, it was not detected, so electrons are observed with a continuous range of energies up to $E_\mathrm{max}$ instead of the small number of discrete lines that energy conservation alone would predict.

The beta-decay spectrum of a radioactive sample shows a continuous distribution of electron energies from nearly zero up to a maximum value, rather than the small number of discrete lines characteristic of alpha and gamma emission. This was a serious problem, because if a nucleus emitted an electron and nothing else, conservation of energy and momentum required the electron to have one definite energy, in the same way that alpha emission gives a definite energy.

Pauli resolved the problem by proposing that a third particle must also be emitted. This particle is electrically neutral, so it is unaffected by electric and magnetic fields and is not detected in the apparatus, and it interacts only through the weak nuclear force, so it passes through the walls of the apparatus almost unhindered. Because the neutrino carries away an unknown and variable share of the released energy, the observed electrons display a continuous range of energies from almost zero up to the maximum $E_\mathrm{max}$ corresponding to the total energy released, which is the right hand end of the curve. The antineutrino, in the case of $\beta^-$ decay, also carries away momentum, so momentum as well as energy is conserved. The Pauli exclusion principle is also relevant, since it means the electrons in the atom already occupy a range of energies rather than a single one.

content.text: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. How did Chadwick apply conservation laws?

For (i), Chadwick was not given the particle, he inferred its properties. Begin with what he actually did: he bombarded beryllium with alpha particles and then let whatever came out strike a block of paraffin containing hydrogen.

Ask what the collisions with the hydrogen nuclei would reveal if the unknown particle had a mass comparable with a proton, and which two conservation laws are needed to extract that mass from the recoil energies.

For (ii), two properties carry the marks. Think first about charge: what would a neutral particle be able to do that a charged one cannot, as it enters matter? Then think about wavelength, using $\lambda = h/mv$ and the size of the spacing between atoms in a material.

** Chadwick used conservation of energy and conservation of momentum. He bombarded a beryllium target with alpha particles and collected the radiation that was produced, then allowed that radiation to collide with the hydrogen nuclei in a block of paraffin. Since the hydrogen nuclei were set moving, he reasoned that the unknown particles must have been transferring energy and momentum to them in elastic collisions, so they must have had a mass comparable with a proton. By measuring the recoil energies and momenta of the ejected protons and applying the conservation laws to each collision, he was able to calculate the mass and other properties of the unknown particle, which had no charge, and so he identified it as the neutron.
**
Part

. The method is to use a collision in which the unknown particle's properties can be read off from what it does to something already known. Alpha particles were fired at a beryllium target; the radiation emitted was then directed at paraffin, which contains a large number of hydrogen atoms, each with a single proton in its nucleus. That radiation knocked protons out of the paraffin, which means it had momentum and had transferred energy in an elastic collision. Assuming conservation of energy and conservation of momentum for each collision, and using the known mass of the proton, the mass of the unknown particle can be solved for; it came out close to the proton mass. Since the radiation was not deflected by electric or magnetic fields it had no charge, and a neutral particle of proton-like mass is the neutron. The examiner report notes that describing the wrong bombarding particles was the common error.
Part

content.text: Outline how the properties of neutrons make them useful in scattering experiments.

** Neutrons have **zero electric charge**, so they are not deflected by the electric field of a nucleus nor repelled by the electrons surrounding it, and they are not stopped by ionisation; they therefore penetrate deeply into matter and reach the nuclei. Their **mass**, close to that of a proton, also gives them a de Broglie wavelength $\lambda = h/mv$ comparable with the interatomic distances in many solids, which makes them ideal for probing the arrangement of atoms in a material, since the diffraction pattern they produce records that spacing.

. Two properties do the work. The first is the zero charge: a charged projectile would be strongly repelled or attracted by the charged particles in matter and would be stopped in the outer electron cloud, whereas a neutral neutron passes through it and interacts only when it comes within about a nuclear diameter of a nucleus, which is why neutron scattering probes nuclei rather than electron shells. The second is the mass, $1.675\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$, close to that of the proton. For a slow neutron of thermal energy, about $0.025\,\mathrm{eV}$, the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda = h/mv$ is about $1.8\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$, comparable with the spacing between atoms in a solid, so the lattice diffracts the neutron and the diffraction pattern reveals the structure of the material.

content.text: Account for the existence of stable isotopes, referring to the forces which act within the atomic nucleus.
Name the forces that act inside a nucleus and, for each, say whether it attracts or repels and over what distance it acts.

The short-range attractive force is what holds the nucleus together. The repulsive force acts between every pair of protons, not merely between neighbours, so its total grows quickly as the number of protons rises.
A neutron adds strong-force attraction but no electrostatic repulsion, so work out what range of neutron numbers can be stable, and what a nucleus does when it falls above or below that range.

Three fundamental forces act within the nucleus. The strong nuclear force is attractive, acts only over very short distances of about $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$, and is very strong, and it binds the nucleons together. The electrostatic force is repulsive between the protons and acts at long range. The weak nuclear force acts only in certain nuclear reactions such as beta decay. A nucleus is stable when the strong nuclear force binding each nucleon is just able to overcome the electrostatic repulsion of the protons, with a small excess of strong force; too few neutrons and the electrostatic repulsion wins, causing alpha emission, and too many neutrons and the nucleus becomes unstable and undergoes beta emission.
Three of the four fundamental forces act within the atomic nucleus, and the existence of stable isotopes is a consequence of the competition between two of them.

The strong nuclear force is the dominant force in the nucleus. It is attractive between every pair of nucleons, protons and neutrons alike, it is enormously stronger than the electrostatic force, and it acts only over very short distances of about $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$, beyond which it falls rapidly to zero. Because it is attractive and acts between all pairs of nucleons, it is the force that binds the nucleus together and is what holds neutrons and protons in a stable arrangement, so the strong nuclear force is a fundamental cause of the existence of stable isotopes.

The electrostatic force acts between the positively charged protons. It is repulsive, and although it is much weaker than the strong nuclear force between a given pair of nucleons, it acts at long range, so a proton repels every other proton in the nucleus, not just its nearest neighbours. In a nucleus containing many protons the total electrostatic repulsion is large, and it is this force that tends to break the nucleus apart. The weak nuclear force is repulsive between protons at extremely short distances and governs the processes of beta decay and the stability issues raised below; it is also the force involved in fusion in stars.

A nucleus is stable when the short-range, very strong, attractive strong nuclear force is just sufficient to overcome the long-range repulsive electrostatic force between all the protons. Every proton must be within about $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$ of every other nucleon, so a given number of protons can only be held together if a sufficient number of neutrons is present to provide the extra strong-force attraction without adding any extra electrostatic repulsion, since the neutron is electrically neutral. Consequently there is a range of neutron numbers for each atomic number, and it is this range that accounts for the existence of stable isotopes: elements with several stable isotopes are those for which several neutron numbers in that range are possible. If a nucleus has too few neutrons the electrostatic repulsion is not sufficiently balanced, and the nucleus is unstable, most commonly emitting an alpha particle because the resulting daughter nucleus has a lower charge-to-mass ratio and so less repulsion. If a nucleus has too many neutrons it is also unstable, most commonly undergoing beta emission so that a neutron is converted into a proton and an electron and an antineutrino, reducing the neutron-to-proton ratio, because the strong nuclear force has a very short range so an excess of neutrons cannot be compensated by extra strong-force attraction.

content.text: 'Important fundamental discoveries in physics often lead to applications which have a significant effect on society.'
Evaluate this statement, with reference to the contributions of Rutherford, Einstein and Fermi to the development of the atomic bomb.
Treat this as three separate contributions and keep them in order, attaching a piece of evidence or a date to each so that they cannot be blurred together.
For each scientist ask what became possible that was not possible before: a target for later experiments, a quantity that could be calculated, or a demonstration that a process could be sustained.

The statement has two clauses - that fundamental discoveries lead to applications, and that those applications have a significant effect on society - so both must be addressed before you judge it. End with the judgement itself.

Rutherford discovered the atomic nucleus and the proton, showing that the atom's mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus; this is the discovery that made nuclear reactions and nuclear energy possible. Einstein's mass-energy equivalence $E = mc^{2}$ provided the quantitative basis for the enormous energy released by a change in mass such as fission. Fermi demonstrated that a neutron alone could be absorbed by a nucleus to produce a heavier nucleus and that a chain reaction of such fission could be sustained and controlled, producing the first controlled nuclear chain reaction. The statement is well supported: these three fundamental discoveries, made for purely scientific reasons, led within decades to the atomic bomb, which had a devastating effect on society.
The statement can be tested by tracing the chain of fundamental discoveries that led to the atomic bomb and then considering its effect on society.

Rutherford's contributions were the discovery of the atomic nucleus and of the proton, made in the first decade of the twentieth century. The gold foil experiment showed that the atom is mostly empty space with its positive charge and most of its mass concentrated in a minute central nucleus, and the later bombardment of nitrogen with alpha particles produced protons, showing that the nucleus contains positively charged particles. This was a purely scientific discovery, made to understand the structure of matter, with no thought of any military application, but it is the essential first step: it established that a tiny fraction of the mass of an atom was stored in a very small region, and therefore that a reaction involving nuclei could release an enormous amount of energy. It also provided the target for neutron bombardment used later by the bomb programmes.

Einstein's contribution was the mass-energy equivalence, $E = mc^{2}$, published in 1905, which states that mass is itself a store of energy. The justification for this is that it supplies the quantitative link between the mass lost in a nuclear reaction and the energy released: when a heavy nucleus splits into lighter nuclei, the total mass of the products is slightly less than the mass of the original nucleus, and that small mass defect is converted directly into a very large quantity of energy, because the speed of light is a very large number. In a heavy nucleus the mass defect per nucleon is a small fraction of a percent, but because the total mass of a nucleus is large and $c^{2}$ is enormous, the energy released is of the order of hundreds of MeV per nucleus. Einstein's equation is what made it possible to predict and to size the yield of a fission weapon, even though Einstein himself did not work on the bomb and did not send the letter that contributed to the Manhattan Project.

Fermi's contribution was the demonstration of nuclear fission and of the possibility of a controlled nuclear chain reaction. In 1938, following the discovery by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann that bombarding uranium with neutrons produced barium, and Irene Curie and Pavel Savitch's observation of the resulting radioactivity, Fermi and Leó Szilard correctly interpreted the result: a heavy uranium nucleus absorbs a neutron, becomes unstable and splits into two medium-mass nuclei, releasing additional neutrons as well as energy. Fermi and Szilard then showed that each fission releases further neutrons, so that if enough uranium is present the process is self-sustaining, a chain reaction, and they demonstrated the first controlled nuclear chain reaction in the graphite pile under the stands of a squash court at the University of Chicago in December 1942, Chicago Pile-1, which proved that a nuclear chain reaction could be produced and controlled. That demonstration is the direct technical precursor of the bomb, because a reactor and a bomb use the same physics, differing only in whether the chain reaction is controlled or uncontrolled. The same work led to the first nuclear power plant, and to the Fermilab accelerator, so the discovery had a peaceful application as well.

The statement is therefore well supported. Each of the three discoveries was made in the course of pure scientific enquiry, motivated by a desire to understand matter and energy rather than to build a weapon, and the interval between the discovery and the bomb was several decades in each case. Together they made the atomic bomb possible within about forty years of Rutherford's gold foil experiment. The effect on society has been profound and double-edged. The immediate effect was the catastrophic loss of life in Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945, together with the psychological shock of a weapon that ended a war and could have ended civilisation, and the long-term effect has been the continuing threat of nuclear annihilation that dominated the Cold War and still governs international relations. The knowledge of fission gained in that effort has also had major beneficial effects, including nuclear power generation, medical imaging and radiotherapy, and the detection of smoke using ionisation. The statement is therefore true in its first clause, but the significance for society has been as much a warning as a benefit, so a fair evaluation would add that such discoveries carry a responsibility to consider their consequences as well as their applications.

content.text: Section A converts temperature into a voltage and section B converts that voltage into a switching output. Establish the divider formula first, then the reference voltage the comparator compares against.
For the value at $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, read the thermistor's resistance off the LOG graph - the vertical axis is logarithmic, so read the decade and minor marks carefully.

For the transfer graph the output can only be $0\\,\mathrm{V}$ or $5\\,\mathrm{V}$, so the curve is a step. Find the switching temperature from the condition $V_t$ equals the reference, and remember that the feedback resistor alters the threshold.

(i) Section A is a potential divider that produces an output voltage $V_t$ which varies with temperature, falling as the temperature rises because the thermistor is an NTC thermistor. (ii) $V_t = 3.57\\,\mathrm{V}$, using $R \approx 4.0\\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ at $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. (iii) Section B is a comparator with hysteresis: the two $10\\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistors hold the inverting input at $2.5\\,\mathrm{V}$, and the output is $0\\,\mathrm{V}$ when $V_t$ is below that and $5\\,\mathrm{V}$ when it is above, so the analogue input is converted into a switching output. $R_3$ provides positive feedback, which is what prevents the output chattering when $V_t$ is near the threshold. (iv) A horizontal line at $0\\,\mathrm{V}$ from $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to about $42^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, then a rapid rise to $5\\,\mathrm{V}$, then a horizontal line at $5\\,\mathrm{V}$ out to $100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
(i) Section A is a potential divider: the thermistor and the $10\\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor are in series between $+5\\,\mathrm{V}$ and $0\\,\mathrm{V}$, with the output taken from their junction.

Because the thermistor is an NTC device its resistance falls as the temperature rises, so the fraction of the supply dropped across the fixed resistor rises and $V_t$ falls. The circuit therefore converts temperature into a voltage.

(ii) Reading the characteristic curve at $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ gives $R_{\text{thermistor}} \approx 4.0\\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$; the vertical axis is logarithmic and the plotted point lies between the $1\\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $10\\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ decades, close to the $4\\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ minor mark.

(iii) The op-amp in section B compares $V_t$ at its non-inverting input with a reference at its inverting input. The two $10\\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistors in section B form a potential divider across the supply, so the inverting input is held at a constant $2.5\\,\mathrm{V}$, and that is the set point.

When $V_t < 2.5\\,\mathrm{V}$, at low temperatures where the thermistor's resistance is large, the non-inverting input is lower than the inverting input and the output saturates low, so $V_o = 0\\,\mathrm{V}$. When $V_t > 2.5\\,\mathrm{V}$ the output saturates high, so $V_o = 5\\,\mathrm{V}$. The circuit therefore converts an analogue quantity into a switching output, which could be used to operate a heater, an alarm or a motor once the temperature passes the set point.

$R_3$, the $100\\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor from the output to the non-inverting input, provides positive feedback. While the output is at $5\\,\mathrm{V}$ it holds the non-inverting input above $2.5\\,\mathrm{V}$, so the input must fall considerably further before the output switches low; while the output is at $0\\,\mathrm{V}$ it holds the non-inverting input below $2.5\\,\mathrm{V}$, so the input must rise considerably further before it switches high. This creates hysteresis, a band between the two switching temperatures, so that small fluctuations of $V_t$ about the set point do not make the output oscillate rapidly between $0\\,\mathrm{V}$ and $5\\,\mathrm{V}$. The large value of $R_3$ also minimises the current it draws from the output.
(iv) While the output is low, $R_3$ is effectively in parallel with the $10\\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor of section A, so the lower arm of the divider has resistance

Switching occurs when $V_t$ reaches the $2.5\\,\mathrm{V}$ reference, that is when $R_{\text{thermistor}} = R_{\text{lower}} = 9.1\\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$. Reading $9.1\\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ off the curve gives about $42^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, so as the temperature rises from $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ the output stays at $0\\,\mathrm{V}$ until about $42^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, then rises to $5\\,\mathrm{V}$ and remains there to $100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The graph of $V_o$ against temperature is therefore a step, not a smooth curve.

content.text: Outline the construction and operation of a relay. Include diagrams in your answer.
A relay is two circuits that never touch electrically. Draw them side by side before you describe anything.
For the marks, name the components - electromagnet and coil, soft iron core, pivot, spring, contacts - and then trace what happens when, and when not, the control current flows.

A relay consists of an electromagnetic coil wound on a soft iron core, an pivoting soft iron armature attracted to the core, a spring to hold the armature away, and a set of electrical contacts. A small current through the coil produces a magnetic field in the core that attracts the armature, moving the contacts. This allows a small current in the control circuit to switch a much larger current in a separate circuit, and to do so with no electrical or mechanical contact between the two circuits.

A relay has two electrically isolated circuits. The control circuit contains a coil of insulated wire wound on a soft iron core, forming an electromagnet, and the switching circuit contains a pivoting soft iron armature, a return spring, and one or more sets of fixed and moving electrical contacts.

In its resting state the spring holds the armature away from the core, so the contacts are in their normal position, for example with the moving contact held clear of the fixed contact by the spring. When a small current is passed through the coil the core becomes magnetised, and the field exerts an attractive force on the armature which pivots towards the core. The movement of the armature carries the moving contact across to the fixed contact, closing the switching circuit. When the control current is removed the coil's field collapses, the spring pulls the armature back and the contacts return to their resting position, opening the circuit.

Because the switching circuit is electrically separate from the control circuit, a small current of a few milliamperes in the control circuit can make and break a much larger current at a much higher voltage in the switching circuit. This means a delicate control or electronic circuit can operate a large motor, heater, lamp or solenoid, which would otherwise require a large switch operated by hand. The relay also provides complete electrical isolation between the two circuits, so the high-voltage circuit can be kept at earth potential, and it allows remote and automatic control from a safe location. The diagrams in a full answer show the two circuits side by side, one containing the battery or control switch and the coil, and the other containing the supply, the load and the contacts, together with a labelled sketch of the electromagnet, armature, spring and contacts.

content.text: There are three inputs, so work through $2^{3} = 8$ rows, evaluating the AND gate and the NOT gate before the OR gate in every row.
A useful check: find the rows in which the two inputs of the OR gate are both 0 - the output must be 0 in exactly those rows.
$O_0 = I_0 \cdot I_1 + \overline{I_2}$, giving $O_0 = 1$ for the input combinations 000, 110 and 111, and $O_0 = 0$ for 001, 010, 011, 100 and 101.

The circuit has three inputs, so there are $2^{3} = 8$ possible input combinations. The two inputs $I_0$ and $I_1$ enter an AND gate, whose output is 1 only when both inputs are 1. $I_2$ enters a NOT gate, whose output is the complement of $I_2$. The outputs of the AND gate and the NOT gate then enter an OR gate, whose output $O_0$ is 1 if either of its inputs is 1.

Evaluating each combination: for 000 the AND gate gives 0 and the NOT gate gives 1, so $O_0 = 1$; for 001 the AND gate gives 0 and the NOT gate gives 0, so $O_0 = 0$; for 010 the AND gate gives 0 and the NOT gate gives 1, so $O_0 = 1$; for 011 the AND gate gives 0 and the NOT gate gives 0, so $O_0 = 0$; for 100 the AND gate gives 0 and the NOT gate gives 1, so $O_0 = 1$; for 101 the AND gate gives 0 and the NOT gate gives 0, so $O_0 = 0$; for 110 the AND gate gives 1 and the NOT gate gives 1, so $O_0 = 1$; for 111 the AND gate gives 1 and the NOT gate gives 0, so $O_0 = 1$. The output is therefore 1 except when $I_0$ or $I_1$ is 0 and $I_2$ is 1, which is the behaviour of an inhibit or NAND-type function.

content.text: What is the function of an input transducer?
The test for an input transducer is whether energy flows FROM the measured quantity INTO the circuit.
Apply that test to each of the two devices in turn, remembering that a component's classification depends on the job it is doing, not on the component itself.

An input transducer converts a physical quantity in the external world - light, temperature, pressure, sound - into an electrical signal, or a change of resistance, that the rest of the system can process.

An input transducer takes energy from the quantity being measured and converts it into a form the processing part of the system can use. Examples: an LDR or photodiode, which convert light into a change of resistance or a current; a thermistor, which converts temperature into a change of resistance; a microphone, which converts a sound wave into a varying voltage; and a pressure-sensitive or strain-gauge resistor, which converts force into a change of resistance. In every case the energy comes from the environment and the output is electrical, so the quantity can be measured without disturbing it.

content.text: What type of transducer is an LED?
An LED is an output transducer: it converts electrical energy into light energy.

An LED delivers energy to the environment as light, so it is an output transducer: electrical energy supplied to it is converted into photons, and the brightness tracks the input current. Because it responds almost instantly to small changes in current it is the usual output device in optical communication links and in electronic displays. The classification depends on the role rather than on the component, so an LED operated in reverse as a photodiode, or a photodiode used to measure light, would instead be an input transducer.

content.text: Analyse the effect of the rapid development of integrated circuits on society.
Make sure your first point is that the rate of development is itself the feature being analysed: quantify it, then relate it to the general development of electronics.
For the applications, choose a small number and for each say what it changed about the way society communicates, works or travels; then balance the answer with the costs.

The number of components on an integrated circuit has roughly doubled every two years since the late 1960s, as described by Moore's law, so the power, memory and processing capacity available at a given cost have increased enormously. This has enabled the personal computer, the mobile phone, the internet, satellite navigation, digital cameras, medical monitoring, electronic control of cars and aircraft, and smart grids, which have transformed communication, commerce, education, healthcare, transport and entertainment, while creating new problems of electronic waste, energy consumption, data privacy and a digital divide.

The development of integrated circuits since the late 1960s has been remarkably rapid, and this rapidity is the essential feature of the technology. A single integrated circuit now contains billions of transistors together with their interconnections on a chip a few centimetres across. The rate of increase is summarised by Moore's law, that the number of components that can be integrated on a chip approximately doubles every two years, so that a device with the processing power of a large computer of the 1970s can now be held in a pocket. Photolithography has advanced from producing features tens of micrometres across to features of a few nanometres, and the cost per transistor has fallen by many orders of magnitude. Other enabling technologies, such as the very large scale integration techniques, the development of CMOS logic, the availability of large volumes of ultrapure silicon, the invention of the laser for photolithography and the growth of automated design software, have all contributed.

This rapid development is closely tied to the development of electronics in general, since an integrated circuit is simply a large number of complete electronic components, transistors, diodes, resistors and capacitors together with their interconnections, fabricated on a single substrate. Because many identical components are fabricated at once and interconnected by depositing thin films rather than by soldering, the cost per component and the time to build a circuit both fall dramatically, which makes it economical to place far more components into a device than could be assembled by hand. The consequence is that an IC-based system costs little, consumes little power, occupies little space and is extremely reliable, because there are no mechanical interconnections to fail and no soldered joints.

The rapid development has enabled a succession of new applications, and these are what have had the greatest effect on society. The microprocessor, made possible by large scale integration, put a computer on a single chip and produced the personal computer, which has transformed work, education, commerce and access to information, and the internet, which has transformed communication, publishing and social organisation. Integrated circuits are the basis of the mobile phone, of digital cameras, of audio and video recording and playback, of the electronic games and entertainment industries, of satellite navigation and of the control systems in motor vehicles, aircraft and modern industrial plant. In medicine they are used in hearing aids, in pacemakers, in patient monitoring and in the control of infusion pumps and ventilators, so that diagnosis and treatment have improved markedly. In agriculture they control irrigation and fertiliser application, and in the environment they are used in weather forecasting, in remote sensing by satellites and in smart grids that reduce energy consumption. The electronics industry now underpins most of the modern economy, and the effects on society are therefore profound.

There are also significant negative effects that must be balanced against these benefits. The manufacture of integrated circuits requires extremely pure silicon, large quantities of water and large amounts of energy, and the chemicals used in etching and cleaning are hazardous, so production has environmental impacts and generates a small but serious volume of toxic waste. The rapid obsolescence that drives the industry produces enormous quantities of electronic waste, much of which is exported to countries where it is dismantled by hand, exposing workers to toxic substances. The ubiquity of cheap, powerful computing raises serious issues of privacy and surveillance, cybercrime and the spread of misinformation, and the energy consumed by data centres and by billions of connected devices is a growing source of greenhouse gas emissions. There is also a digital divide, because those who cannot afford the latest devices are further disadvantaged in education and employment. Overall, however, the effect of the rapid development of integrated circuits on society has been strongly positive, and the same feature that makes the technology so powerful, its relentless advance, also requires regulation and recycling to keep its costs and impacts under control.
